Senses.Explanation: A fixed listing string naming the four constituents of body and world, asked about, traced to source, and scattered at death throughout the records. Hongzhi Zhengjue tells the assembly that the body apart from earth, water, fire, and wind is no compound, the wise apart from seeing, hearing, and knowing no divided mind; Dahui Zonggao, asked whether the true body possesses the four, answers that it does, and to what the true body is, answers with the string itself; and Zhongfeng Mingben works it into his instruction: pinched together the four constituents stand like an iron mountain, let go the seeing-heaving-knowing sinks like a jade sea. Chijue Daochong instructs the head monk that the traveler who has not seen through self is drowned in the coarse four constituents and flows on in birth-abiding-change-perishing; Hengchuan Rugong warns the monks not to take the unmoved thought at the scattering of the four as it; Zhuanyu Guanheng traces the body's source back through parents and eons to the constituents' merging birth, making the four the source of the body and its vessel world; Liangting Jingting, at the coffin, tells the departed lady she has lifted off the flesh-bundle and settled the four constituents in one stroke; and Tianran Hanshi, in his treatise reading, holds them neither affirmed nor denied — not mind, not empty, not the four; just mind, just empty, just the four.
